title: The Argument About the Bridge
learning_objectives: Unseen transfer check at the top band: read a new text alone and reason about two opposing views
Identify the strongest argument on each side using evidence
Recognise a compromise and evaluate whether it is fair
parent_prompts: UNSEEN CHECK: do not preview. One solo read, then the questions. Record in parent.html > Evidence > Unseen-text check. Note whether the child can state BOTH sides fairly before choosing one.

pages.text: The footbridge over the canal at the end of Mai's street had been closed for six weeks, since the day a council engineer in a yellow jacket walked across it, stopped in the middle, knelt, and then walked back rather faster than she had come. A sign appeared the next morning: CLOSED FOR SAFETY. Two weeks after that, a letter came to every house. The bridge, it said, could be repaired for a great deal of money, or demolished for rather less, and the council wished to know what residents thought. A meeting would be held in the school hall on Thursday.
pages.illustration_brief: A small iron footbridge over a canal with a barrier and a CLOSED sign; a figure in a yellow jacket kneeling mid-span; terraced houses behind.
pages.audio_script: The footbridge over the canal at the end of Mai's street had been closed for six weeks, since the day a council engineer in a yellow jacket walked across it, stopped in the middle, knelt, and then walked back rather faster than she had come. A sign appeared the next morning: CLOSED FOR SAFETY. Two weeks after that, a letter came to every house. The bridge, it said, could be repaired for a great deal of money, or demolished for rather less, and the council wished to know what residents thought. A meeting would be held in the school hall on Thursday.
pages.image_alt: An old arched footbridge over a canal with a yellow barrier across it and an engineer in a yellow jacket.

pages.text: Mai went with her father, expecting to be bored, and was not. The hall was full. The first to speak was Mr Duc from the corner shop, who was for demolition. "That bridge," he said, "is a hundred and ten years old. It was built for people walking to a factory that closed before I was born. The road bridge is four hundred metres away. Four hundred metres! The money would pave every path in the park, twice. We are being asked to spend a fortune so that people can save five minutes." There was a murmur that sounded like agreement. Mai found herself nodding.
pages.illustration_brief: A packed school hall; a stout man at a microphone gesturing widely; rows of listening faces.
pages.audio_script: Mai went with her father, expecting to be bored, and was not. The hall was full. The first to speak was Mr Duc from the corner shop, who was for demolition. That bridge, he said, is a hundred and ten years old. It was built for people walking to a factory that closed before I was born. The road bridge is four hundred metres away. Four hundred metres! The money would pave every path in the park, twice. We are being asked to spend a fortune so that people can save five minutes. There was a murmur that sounded like agreement. Mai found herself nodding.
pages.image_alt: A packed meeting hall; a shopkeeper at the microphone speaking for demolition.

pages.text: Then old Mrs Lien stood up, with some difficulty, holding the chair in front. She did not use the microphone and the hall went quiet to hear her. "Four hundred metres," she said, "is nothing to Mr Duc. To me it is twenty minutes each way, with a stick, along a road with no pavement on the canal side. I have crossed that bridge to the clinic every Tuesday for thirty-one years. Since it closed I have missed four appointments. My grandson takes me when he can. He cannot always." She sat down. Nobody murmured. Mai stopped nodding and found she did not know what to do with her hands.
pages.illustration_brief: A frail elderly woman standing at her chair, hand on the seat back, speaking without a microphone; the hall silent; Mai in the audience, still.

Nobody murmured. Mai stopped nodding and found she did not know what to do with her hands.
pages.image_alt: An old woman holding the chair in front of her, the hall quiet as she speaks without a microphone.

pages.text: Others spoke. A young father said the road bridge had no proper crossing and he would not push a pram along it. A woman from the far side said the schoolchildren used the footbridge and would otherwise walk the road. Mr Duc said, reasonably, that a crossing on the road bridge would cost a fraction of the repair and solve both problems. Mrs Lien said, from her chair, that a crossing did not shorten four hundred metres. Round it went. Mai noticed that both sides were right about the facts. Mr Duc was right about the money. Mrs Lien was right about the distance. The argument was not about facts. It was about which facts mattered more, and to whom.
pages.illustration_brief: Several speakers in quick succession: a father with a pram, a woman pointing across the canal; Mai looking from one side of the hall to the other.

vocabulary.definition: An agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wanted so that both can accept the result.
vocabulary.example: The compromise was one hour of television, not none and not three.

pages.image_alt: A young father with a pram, a woman pointing across the canal, and others waiting to speak.

pages.text: The engineer in the yellow jacket spoke last, and she said something nobody had asked. The bridge, she explained, was closed because of its deck: the iron plates people walked on had rusted through in places. The great arched girders underneath, the part that actually held it up, were sound. "Replacing the whole bridge is the expensive option," she said. "Replacing the deck alone is perhaps a third of that. It would not be as pretty. It would be a plain steel walkway on the old arches. But it would be open by spring." She sat down. The hall was quiet in a different way now, the way of people doing sums in their heads.
pages.illustration_brief: The engineer with a simple diagram on an easel: an arch with a rusted deck on top, then the same arch with a plain new deck.

pages.image_alt: The engineer pointing at a drawing: the arches are sound, only the deck on top is worn.

pages.text: Mr Duc spoke first, and Mai respected him for what he said. "A third," he said slowly. "With a proper crossing on the road bridge as well, for the prams, that is still less than half of what we were told. I can live with a third." Mrs Lien did not stand this time. "I do not need it to be pretty," she said. "I need it to be there on Tuesday." The vote, when it came, was not close.
pages.illustration_brief: Mr Duc, calmer, one hand raised; Mrs Lien nodding from her seat; hands going up around the hall.

pages.image_alt: The shopkeeper speaking again, a tally on a board showing one third, and Mai listening.

pages.text: Walking home, Mai tried to work out why she had changed her mind twice in one evening and whether that made her weak. Her father thought about it for the length of the street. "You did not change your mind about facts," he said. "Mr Duc's facts were true at the start and true at the end. You changed your mind about what the facts weighed. That is not weakness. That is what listening is for. The people to worry about are the ones who came in knowing and left the same."
pages.illustration_brief: Mai and her father walking home under streetlights along the canal path, the closed bridge dark behind them.

pages.text: The new deck opened in April. It was, as promised, not pretty: grey steel plates with a raised pattern for grip, bolted onto arches that were older than anyone in the street. On the first Tuesday, Mai happened to be at her window at ten and saw Mrs Lien cross it, stick and all, at exactly the speed she had always crossed it. It took her, Mai counted, one minute and forty seconds. She had never thought before about how much could fit inside one minute and forty seconds, or how far it was to walk round.
pages.illustration_brief: Spring: the old arches with a plain new grey deck; Mrs Lien with her stick halfway across; Mai at an upstairs window.

quiz.prompt: What was Mr Duc's main argument for demolishing the bridge?

options.text: The repair cost a fortune to save five minutes when the road bridge was 400 metres away
It blocked the view of his shop

quiz.explanation: Page 2: the road bridge is four hundred metres away; we are being asked to spend a fortune so that people can save five minutes.

quiz.prompt: Why did Mrs Lien's speech stop the murmuring?

options.text: She showed that 'five minutes' was twenty minutes and missed clinic visits for someone who could not walk far
People are always quiet for old people

quiz.explanation: Page 3: four hundred metres is twenty minutes each way with a stick, and she had missed four clinic appointments.

quiz.prompt: What did Mai notice about the argument on page 4?

options.text: Both sides were right about the facts; the disagreement was about which facts mattered more, and to whom

quiz.explanation: Page 4: the argument was not about facts. It was about which facts mattered more, and to whom.

quiz.prompt: Why did the engineer's information change the vote?

options.text: It offered a cheaper option, a new deck on the sound old arches, that met most of both sides' needs
She said the bridge was about to collapse
She offered to fix it for free

quiz.explanation: Page 5: the arches were sound and a new deck alone was about a third of the cost. Page 6: Mr Duc could live with a third and Mrs Lien did not need it to be pretty.

quiz.prompt: What did Mai's father mean by 'the people to worry about are the ones who came in knowing and left the same'?

options.text: Changing your view when you hear better reasons is listening, not weakness; refusing to change is the real problem
People who stay too long at meetings

quiz.explanation: Page 7: you changed your mind about what the facts weighed; that is what listening is for.

quiz.prompt: Was the final decision a compromise? Which option best explains why?

options.text: Yes: Mr Duc gave up demolition but got a lower cost and a road crossing; Mrs Lien gave up the pretty bridge but got it open
No: Mrs Lien got everything she wanted
No: Mr Duc got everything he wanted

quiz.explanation: Page 6 shows each side accepting less than their first position; page 8 shows the result: a plain deck, open, on the old arches.

quiz.prompt: Explain both sides of the argument fairly, as if you agreed with each, then say what the engineer added and whether you think the result was fair.
quiz.rubric: not yet: picks a side only; with support: both sides in outline with prompting; independent: states cost/distance case and access/safety case each in its strongest form, explains the deck-only option, and gives a reasoned verdict on fairness
quiz.explanation: For the unseen check, the key skill is stating the side you disagree with fairly before judging; note whether the child could.

off_screen_prompt: Think of a disagreement at home or school. Say the other person's strongest reason out loud, fairly, before saying your own.
